correction.text: Headlights are required from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, whenever there is not enough light, and whenever you cannot see people or vehicles clearly at one thousand feet.

narration.text: This lesson opens the chapter on special driving conditions with night driving. Night driving is always harder and more hazardous than daytime driving because you see less, later and not as far, and oncoming headlight glare adds to the difficulty. We will cover how to set your speed at night, how to handle glare, what to avoid, why pedestrians need extra attention, when the law requires headlights, when to switch between high and low beams, and how the handbook describes fatal crashes in the evening hours. Each rule helps make up for what darkness takes away.

lines.text: Look down and right at glare.

narration.text: At night, always be able to stop within the distance your headlights light up, and keep your speed under control and within posted limits. Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; look down toward the right side of your lane, using the edge line or center line as a guide. Never wear sunglasses when driving at night, and keep the windshield clean inside and out. Pedestrians are hard to see at night, so stay especially watchful for them after dark. These four habits together keep your eyes and your speed matched to what you can actually see.

lines.text: Half hour after sunset to before sunrise.
Low light or one thousand feet of view.
When a traffic device directs it.

narration.text: Headlights are required by law from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, whenever there is not enough light, and whenever people or vehicles cannot be seen clearly at one thousand feet. Headlights are also required when an official traffic control device directs you to use them, and using them in rain, snow or fog is advisable. So the requirement is not tied only to darkness: low light, limited visibility and posted directions all count. Do not drive with only the parking lights on, because parking lights alone do not meet the rule.

lines.text: Dim five hundred feet before oncoming.

narration.text: Use high beams in open country at night, but switch to low beams at least five hundred feet before meeting an oncoming vehicle and three hundred feet before reaching a vehicle you are following. High beams belong in open country at night, but you must dim to low beams at least five hundred feet before an oncoming vehicle and at least three hundred feet behind a vehicle you follow. You may flash your headlights to warn a driver ahead that you plan to pass. The two distances protect two different drivers: the one coming toward you and the one ahead of you.

Here is the trap. Two distances apply to dimming, and they are easy to swap. For a vehicle coming toward you, switch to low beams at least five hundred feet before you meet it. For a vehicle you are following, switch to low beams at least three hundred feet before you reach it. The larger number goes with the oncoming driver. If a question asks about a car ahead going your way, think three hundred; if it asks about a car coming at you, think five hundred. In both cases, at least means you may dim earlier, never later.

Here is a quick check: you are following another car at night with your high beams on. How close may you get before you must dim them? Recall both distances before reading on. You must switch to low beams at least three hundred feet before reaching a vehicle you are following. The other distance, five hundred feet, applies to an oncoming vehicle. Remember that the handbook also reports that from twenty fifteen to twenty nineteen, two hundred seventy-six fatal crashes happened between six and nine in the evening, nineteen percent of all fatal crashes in Nevada.

lines.text: Headlight hours are set by law.
Dim for oncoming and followed cars.

narration.text: To review, night driving is harder because you see less, later and not as far, with glare added. Stop within your headlight range, look down and right at glare, skip sunglasses, keep the glass clean and watch for pedestrians. Headlights are required from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, in low light, when you cannot see clearly at one thousand feet, and when a traffic device says so; they are advisable in rain, snow or fog. Dim at least five hundred feet before oncoming cars and three hundred feet behind cars you follow, and never drive on parking lights alone.

Braking on ice depends on whether your car has ABS.
Studded tires are legal only during set dates.

reasoning.text: Without ABS, brake with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern; with ABS, hold firm, continuous pressure.

result.text: This driver uses gentle touch-and-release braking to slow and stop safely.

narration.text: This lesson covers bad weather. The most important thing in bad weather is to slow down, since stopping distances on slippery roads can be two to ten times longer than on dry pavement. Nevada weather can change suddenly with wind, rain and snowstorms, and in fog, rain or snow other drivers struggle to see just as you do, so leave extra space and watch the tail lights ahead. We will cover winter equipment, starting and braking on snow and ice, braking with and without ABS, the studded-tire season and what skidding means.

lines.text: Chains, snow tires or all-weather radials.

narration.text: For snowy or icy roads, fit chains, snow tires or all-weather radials, and remember that even well-equipped vehicles can slide. On snow or ice, start very slowly, test your brakes gently to learn how well you can stop, and begin slowing well before intersections and turns. No speed is completely safe on snow and ice, because conditions change with sun, shade and sanding from one block or stretch of road to the next. On snow and ice avoid sudden changes in speed or direction, keep windows and windshield clear, and allow extra time to reach your destination.

On slippery roads, gentle braking with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern helps you stop safely, but a vehicle with ABS needs firm, continuous pedal pressure for the anti-lock feature to work. Without ABS, brake on ice with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern, while with ABS you hold firm, continuous pressure on the pedal; check the owner's manual. So the right technique depends on the car. The owner's manual tells you which kind of braking system your car has, and the two methods are opposites. Check the owner's manual for your own car.

lines.text: Studs only October one to April thirty.

narration.text: Skidding means the tires have lost traction; it happens most on ice or packed snow but also on wet pavement or gravel. Skid recovery differs by braking and steering system and by four-wheel or front-wheel drive, so the owner's manual is the source for your vehicle, and in any emergency stay calm. Studded snow tires may be used only from October one through April thirty; tires with retractable studs are legal all year, but the studs may be engaged only within those dates. So the tire may stay on the car, but the studs follow the calendar.

lines.text: No ABS: light touch and release.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Gentle touch-and-release braking is the right method on ice without ABS, so drivers sometimes use it in every car. With ABS, the opposite is true: the anti-lock feature needs firm, continuous pressure on the pedal to work. When a question names a car with ABS, the answer is firm, steady pressure; when it names a car without ABS, the answer is a slow, light touch and release. Equipment does not make ice safe either: even well-equipped vehicles can slide, and no speed is completely safe on snow and ice.

Here is a quick check: during which dates may studded snow tires be used in Nevada? Recall the season before reading on. They may be used only from October one through April thirty. Tires with retractable studs are legal all year, but the studs may be engaged only within those same dates. Whatever tires you use, slow down first in bad weather, because stopping distances on slippery roads can be two to ten times longer than on dry pavement, and remember that even well-equipped vehicles can slide on snow and ice. Slow down first in bad weather.

To review, slow down first in bad weather, because stopping distances on slippery roads can be two to ten times longer than on dry pavement, and leave extra space in fog, rain or snow. Fit chains, snow tires or all-weather radials, start slowly, test your brakes and begin slowing early, knowing that even well-equipped cars can slide and no speed is completely safe on ice. Without ABS, brake with a light touch and release; with ABS, hold firm, steady pressure. Skidding means lost traction, the owner's manual explains recovery, and studded tires are allowed only from October one through April thirty.

why_how.text: Emergencies such as brake failure or a stuck gas pedal require specific steps, and the wrong one can make things worse.
A fire, failed steering or an oncoming car each has its own response.

scenario.text: A driver's gas pedal sticks on a highway, and pressing it hard and releasing does not free it.

reasoning.text: If the pedal stays stuck, shift to neutral, brake, and pull off to the right and stop, never shifting into park.

result.text: The driver shifts to neutral, brakes, and pulls off to the right to stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should shift into park when the brakes or the gas pedal fail.

correction.text: With failed brakes you shift to a lower gear and use the parking brake, while with a stuck gas pedal you shift to neutral and brake; in neither case do you shift into park.

memory_support.text: Brakes fail: pump, park brake, gear down; never park.

prompt.text: How far should you move away from a vehicle fire you cannot stop?

rationale.text: Never use water on a vehicle fire; use a chemical extinguisher, sand or dirt, and if the fire cannot be stopped, move at least one hundred feet away.

narration.text: This lesson covers vehicle emergencies: failed brakes, a stuck gas pedal, wet brakes, failed wipers or headlights, smoke or fire, failed steering, and a vehicle coming at you in your lane. Each one has its own steps, and several look alike, so it pays to learn them in order. In any emergency, stay calm. We will also look at using a lower gear on long downhill stretches, which protects your brakes before anything goes wrong. As you go, notice that two emergencies share one rule: never shift into park while the car is still moving.

lines.text: Brakes fail: pump, parking brake, lower gear.
Pedal sticks: tap, then neutral and brake.

narration.text: If the brakes fail, pump the pedal; if they still do not respond, use the parking brake and shift to a lower gear if possible, but never shift into park. Use a lower gear when driving downhill for long stretches to avoid wearing out the brakes. If the gas pedal sticks, quickly press it hard and release; if it stays stuck, shift to neutral, brake, and pull off to the right and stop, never shifting into park. After driving through deep water, test your brakes; dry them by driving slowly in low gear while braking lightly, testing about every two hundred feet.

lines.text: Wipers fail: slow, window down, pull off.
Headlights fail: use parking lights or flashers.
Leave the road as soon as possible.

narration.text: When the wipers stop working during heavy rain or snow, reduce speed, roll the window down and lean out to see, and get off the highway to the right and stop as soon as you can. If the headlights fail, slow down and leave the roadway as soon as possible, using parking lights, turn signals or four-way flashers, which usually still work, to guide you. Both failures take away your ability to see or be seen, so the response in both cases is the same in spirit: slow down and get off the road safely before going any farther.

lines.text: Smoke: slow, pull off, ignition off.
Open the hood with extreme caution.

narration.text: If you see smoke rising from the engine area, slow, get off the road and shut off the ignition immediately, and open the hood with extreme caution. Never use water on a vehicle fire, because burning gasoline floats and spreads. Use a chemical extinguisher, or sand or dirt, and if the fire cannot be stopped, move at least one hundred feet away. So the order is: get off the road, shut off the ignition, approach the hood carefully, smother the fire with the right material, and leave the area if the fire gets out of control.

lines.text: Steering fails: ease off the gas.
Oncoming car: slow, horn, lights, go right.

narration.text: If steering fails, ease off the accelerator; if the car holds its lane, slow and brake gently with flashers on, but brake hard if it heads off the road or toward a vehicle or pedestrian. If a vehicle comes at you in your lane, slow down, sound the horn, flash your headlights and pull as far right as is safe, without swerving into the lane it left. Pulling right while slowing, sounding the horn and flashing the lights is the whole response, and swerving left is never part of it. If the car holds its lane, the flashers warn other drivers while you slow and brake gently to a stop.

lines.text: Brake failure: lower gear and parking brake.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Brake failure and a stuck gas pedal both feel like losing control, and their steps are easy to mix up. With failed brakes, you pump the pedal, then use the parking brake and shift to a lower gear. With a stuck gas pedal, you press it hard and release, then shift to neutral and brake. The shared rule is that in neither case do you shift into park. So ask what failed: if the brakes will not stop the car, gear down; if the engine will not stop pushing, take it out of gear into neutral. Never shift into park while the car is moving.

lines.text: How far away should you go?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your vehicle catches fire and you cannot put it out. How far away should you move? Recall the distance before reading on. Move at least one hundred feet away from the vehicle. Before that, the steps are to slow, get off the road, shut off the ignition and open the hood only with extreme caution. Never use water, because burning gasoline floats and spreads. A chemical extinguisher, sand or dirt can smother a small fire, but once it is out of control, distance is the only safe answer. Stay calm in any emergency.

lines.text: Never shift into park while moving.
Get off the road when you cannot see.
No water on fires; distance if needed.

narration.text: To sum up, if brakes fail, pump them, then use the parking brake and a lower gear, and use a lower gear on long downhills to spare the brakes. If the gas pedal sticks, tap it, then shift to neutral, brake and pull off, never into park. Dry wet brakes in low gear with light braking. If wipers or headlights fail, slow and get off the road. For smoke, pull off and shut off the ignition; never use water on a fire, and move one hundred feet away if needed. If steering fails, ease off and brake as the situation demands, and never swerve into the lane an oncoming car has left.

why_how.text: Running off the road causes serious single-vehicle crashes that account for many Nevada deaths.
Flash floods are a real risk in Nevada, and most flood deaths involve vehicles.
Floating vehicles are very hard to escape, which is why the depth figures matter.

scenario.text: A driver comes to a road covered by moving water that looks only a few inches deep.

reasoning.text: A car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only six inches of water, and the depth and whether the road beneath has washed out cannot be judged.

result.text: The driver turns around and takes another route or waits for the water to go down.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should swerve straight back onto the road after drifting onto the shoulder.

correction.text: Do not swerve back; stay on the shoulder until fully in control, then ease back onto the road.

memory_support.text: Turn around; water hides its depth.

prompt.text: Floodwater over a road is about two feet deep. Could it float most vehicles?

answer.text: Yes; most vehicles can float in two feet of water or less.

rationale.text: Most vehicles can float in two feet of water or less, and a car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only six inches of water.

narration.text: This lesson covers running off the road, tire blowouts, disabled vehicles and flash floods. Running off the road causes serious single-vehicle crashes that account for many Nevada deaths, with fatigue, inattention and speeding as major factors. Blowouts call for a calm, steady response. And Nevada's dry climate makes flash floods likely, especially in summer storms, spring thaw or long rains. We will look at how to recover from each situation, what to do with a disabled vehicle, and why the handbook's flood rule is so simple: turn around.

lines.text: Stay calm; lift off the gas.

narration.text: If you drift onto the shoulder, stay calm, lift off the gas, brake only carefully, grip the wheel firmly, and do not swerve back. Stay on the shoulder until you are fully in control, then ease back onto the road. Running off the road causes serious single-vehicle crashes that account for many Nevada deaths, and fatigue, inattention and speeding are major factors in them. So the order is calm, off the gas, careful braking, a firm grip, staying on the shoulder, and only then easing back. Fatigue, inattention and speeding are the major factors behind these run-off-road crashes.

lines.text: Blowout: grip, ease off, no brakes.
Disabled: off the road, warn, tow.

narration.text: In a tire blowout, grip the wheel firmly and ease off the gas without hitting the brakes, then brake gently only once the vehicle is under control and has slowed. After a blowout, signal, pull safely off the road and warn others with parking lights or flashers. With a disabled vehicle, get all four wheels off the roadway if possible, warn other drivers with parking lights, flashers or flares, and have it towed as soon as you can. Control comes first in each case, and then getting off the roadway. Use parking lights, flashers or flares to warn others.

lines.text: Blowout: no brakes until in control.
Both: grip the wheel, lift off the gas.

narration.text: Here is a trap with two similar emergencies. In a blowout you must not hit the brakes until the vehicle is under control, whereas after drifting onto the shoulder you may brake, but only carefully. In both cases grip the wheel firmly and lift off the gas. The difference is about the brakes: the blowout calls for no braking at first, the shoulder drift allows careful braking. When a question describes a sudden loss of air in a tire, think no brakes yet; when it describes wheels dropping onto the shoulder, think careful braking and no swerving.

lines.text: Under one inch can cost control.
Two feet can float most vehicles.
Six inches can push a fast car off.

narration.text: More than half of all flash flood deaths involve vehicles, and less than one inch of water can make a driver lose control. Most vehicles can float in two feet of water or less, and a car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only six inches of water. Nevada's dry climate makes flash floods likely, especially in summer storms, spring thaw or long rains, and floating vehicles drift toward deeper, faster water where top-heavy ones may roll. So even shallow-looking water on a road can be far more dangerous than it seems.

title.text: What to do at a flood

lines.text: Never drive through a flooded road.

narration.text: Never try to drive through a flooded road; turn around and take another route or wait for the water to go down, since its depth and whether the road beneath has washed out cannot be judged. If your vehicle stalls in rising flood water and it is safe, leave it at once and get to higher ground. The only sure flood safety rule is to turn around and stay off flooded roads, and you must never drive around barricades that officials have put up. Be extra careful about floods at night, never cross flowing streams, and move to higher ground when water rises fast.

lines.text: How much can float a car?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how much water can float most vehicles? Recall the figures before reading on. Most vehicles can float in two feet of water or less. Even less is needed to cause trouble: a car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only six inches of water, and less than one inch can make a driver lose control. That is why the handbook's only sure flood rule is to turn around and stay off flooded roads, and never to drive around barricades that officials have put up. Floating vehicles drift toward deeper, faster water, where top-heavy ones may roll.

To review, after drifting onto the shoulder stay calm, lift off the gas, brake carefully and ease back only when in control. In a blowout, grip the wheel and ease off the gas without braking until under control, then signal, pull off and warn others. Get a disabled vehicle off the roadway, warn drivers and have it towed. Flash floods are likely in Nevada; under an inch of water can cost control, six inches can push a fast car off the road and two feet can float most vehicles. Never drive through or around flooded roads, and leave a stalled car in rising water if it is safe.

why_how.text: Work zones narrow lanes and bring stopped traffic, and penalties there are higher.
Nevada law requires drivers to slow down and move over for stopped emergency and service vehicles.
Signed shoulders give certain emergency vehicles a clear path, and other drivers may not stop there.

scenario.text: A driver on a two-lane-each-way highway sees a tow truck stopped on the right shoulder with its lights on.

reasoning.text: Slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit, be ready to stop, and if possible move into a lane not next to the stopped vehicle.

result.text: The driver slows below the limit and, with the left lane clear, moves over before passing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an orange speed limit sign in a work zone is the legal limit.

correction.text: A black and white speed limit sign is the legal limit, while an orange one is only an advisory, safer speed.

prompt.text: Which vehicles may drive on a paved highway shoulder where signs authorize it?

answer.text: Certain emergency vehicles, such as police, fire engines, ambulances, tow cars, coroner vehicles and transit buses.

rationale.text: Some emergency vehicles may use a signed paved shoulder, including police, fire engines, ambulances, incident management vehicles, tow cars, coroner vehicles and public transit buses.

narration.text: This lesson covers two situations where drivers must give extra room: highway work zones and stopped emergency or service vehicles. Work zones are marked with orange signs, cones and barrels; lanes narrow, surfaces are rough and traffic may stop completely, so stay alert and expect stopped cars ahead. Nevada also sets a clear duty for drivers approaching stopped emergency, utility and service vehicles. Finally, we look at highway shoulders marked for emergency use, who may drive on them and who may not stop on them.

lines.text: Black and white is the legal limit.

narration.text: Speeding fines double in work zones; black and white speed limit signs are regulatory, while orange speed limit signs are advisory and suggest slower, safer speeds. Moving barriers or signs to drive onto a closed road is illegal and carries double penalties for work-zone violations. Whenever you see orange signs, slow down, watch for workers and equipment, follow flaggers' instructions and merge carefully and cooperatively. Visibility in work zones may be lower, especially at night, so do not drive tired and watch for sleepy drivers; flaggers and pilot cars often control traffic.

lines.text: Proceed with caution; be ready to stop.
Move over a lane if possible.

narration.text: When approaching a stopped emergency, utility or service vehicle such as a police car, tow truck, NDOT vehicle or garbage truck, slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit, proceed with caution and be ready to stop. When passing such a stopped vehicle, move if possible into a lane not next to the one it occupies, unless road, traffic or weather conditions make that unsafe or impossible. The slow-down duty also applies when approaching a vehicle showing non-flashing blue lights in certain circumstances and when someone is repairing a vehicle.

lines.text: Ordinary drivers may not stop there.
In effect since January one, twenty twenty-four.

narration.text: Some emergency vehicles may drive on a paved highway shoulder where signs authorize it, including police, fire engines and ambulances, traffic incident management vehicles, tow cars, coroner vehicles and public transit buses. Drivers of non-emergency vehicles may not stop on a highway shoulder marked for emergency use. The shoulder-use rule for emergency vehicles took effect on January one, twenty twenty-four. So a signed emergency shoulder is for the listed emergency vehicles, not a place for other drivers to stop.

Here is the trap. In a work zone you may see two kinds of speed signs. A black and white speed limit sign in a work zone is the legal limit, while an orange one is only an advisory, safer speed. Drivers sometimes treat the orange sign as the law or ignore it as decoration; it is advice for a safer speed, while the black and white sign is the enforceable limit. Either way, remember that speeding fines double in work zones, and that moving barriers to drive onto a closed road carries double penalties too. Moving barriers onto a closed road also brings double penalties.

Here is a quick check: on a highway with a shoulder signed for emergency use, which vehicles may drive on it? Recall the list before reading on. Certain emergency vehicles may use it where signs authorize it: police, fire engines and ambulances, traffic incident management vehicles, tow cars, coroner vehicles and public transit buses. Drivers of non-emergency vehicles may not stop on a shoulder marked for emergency use. This rule took effect on January one, twenty twenty-four. Police, fire engines and ambulances are among the vehicles listed.

lines.text: Orange signs: slow, watch, follow flaggers.

narration.text: To sum up, work zones are marked by orange signs, cones and barrels, where lanes narrow and traffic may stop. Slow down, watch for workers, follow flaggers and merge carefully, and stay alert at night. Speeding fines double there, black and white signs are the legal limit and orange signs advise a safer speed, and moving barriers carries double penalties. For stopped emergency, utility and service vehicles, slow below the limit, be ready to stop and move over a lane if possible. Keep signed emergency shoulders clear for the listed emergency vehicles.
